newEntries.name: The Christian Right
newEntries.statusDescription: A political movement carried by organizations across several church bodies, not a church or a confession. Its record is strong, but what it formed in people beyond politics is thin, and this entry says so.
newEntries.sourcing: Moderate to rich. The 1980 Dallas briefing is documented. So are the Christian Coalition's founding and the Moral Majority's end, both in 1989, and the Faith and Freedom Coalition's founding in 2009. The Moral Majority's 1979 founding date is not yet verified. Later historians (Du Mez, Whitehead and Perry, Stewart, Gorski) studied the movement independently.
newEntries.floorNote: There is no confession of its own to test. The movement was built as a coalition. Its first leaders included Catholics, a Jew and fundamentalist Baptists, joined by shared political and moral aims rather than a shared creed. This reading is provisional until its sources are verified.
newEntries.relationsSummary: Drew heavily on fundamentalist and evangelical churches without becoming any one of them. Its organizations were the Moral Majority (1979–1989), the Christian Coalition (from 1989) and the Faith and Freedom Coalition (from 2009). Rush Limbaugh's national radio program from 1988 and Fox News from 1996 carried its shared story as media outlets, not as churches.
newEntries.why: In August 1980 the candidate Ronald Reagan spoke at a briefing in Dallas. He told the evangelical leaders on the platform: 'I know this is a nonpartisan gathering, and so I know that you can't endorse me, but I only brought that up because I want you to know that I endorse you and what you're doing.' The Moral Majority had been founded the year before. It closed in 1989, and the Christian Coalition was founded the same year. In 2009 Ralph Reed, the Christian Coalition's first executive director, founded the Faith and Freedom Coalition.
